faq.a: Blood flows from high‑pressure left ventricle to right ventricle throughout systole, creating turbulence heard as a holosystolic murmur.
faq.q: Why does a ventricular septal defect cause a holosystolic murmur?

faq.a: It indicates an atrial septal defect because right‑sided filling is delayed by left‑to‑right shunt, keeping the split constant.
faq.q: What is the clinical significance of a fixed split second heart sound?

faq.a: Increased left‑atrial pressure pushes the septum primum against the septum secundum, functionally sealing the opening.
faq.q: How does the foramen ovale close after birth?

exam: A newborn presents with a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border – what embryologic error explains this and what is the next investigation? — Look for a ventricular septal defect (failure of interventricular septum formation); obtain an echocardiogram to define size and shunt.

A 3‑year‑old has easy fatigability, a wide fixed split S2, and a systolic ejection murmur – which defect is most likely and how does it arise? — Atrial septal defect; failure of septum primum and secundum to fuse, leaving a persistent foramen ovale.

Why is early closure of a patent ductus arteriosus dangerous in a pre‑term infant? — Sudden loss of a low‑resistance pathway raises systemic pressure, precipitating heart failure; prostaglandin E1 may be needed if ductal‑dependent lesion is suspected.

In a child with tetralogy of Fallot, why is a ‘boot‑shaped’ heart seen on X‑ray? — Overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy enlarge the right heart silhouette, creating the characteristic shape.

A patient with sickle cell disease develops acute chest pain and a new murmur – what congenital lesion should you suspect worsening and why? — A previously silent ventricular septal defect may become hemodynamically significant due to increased pulmonary pressures from sickle‑cell pulmonary hypertension.

Explain why a high‑altitude environment can unmask a previously silent atrial septal defect. — Reduced ambient oxygen raises pulmonary vascular resistance, increasing right‑to‑left shunt through the ASD, causing cyanosis.

When echocardiography is unavailable, how can you differentiate a large VSD from a small one clinically? — Large VSD produces a loud, harsh murmur with signs of heart failure; small VSD gives a softer murmur without failure.
What pharmacologic agent is avoided in a patient with a large VSD and why? — Beta‑blockers are avoided early because they may reduce cardiac output in the setting of a left‑to‑right shunt.
ai.title: Cardiac Development
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The heart forms from a linear tube that folds and septates into four chambers. Key steps include looping, atrial and ventricular septation, and outflow tract division, each vulnerable to congenital defects.

b: Outflow tract divides into aorta and pulmonary artery
sections.p: During the third week of gestation a mesodermal heart tube forms and begins rhythmic contractions. It undergoes rightward looping, septation, and remodeling to become a four‑chambered organ.

b: Septum primum grows from the roof of the primitive atrium
Septum secundum forms posteriorly, leaving the foramen ovale
sections.p: By the end of the eighth week the heart sits in the middle mediastinum, apex pointing left. The interatrial septum (septum primum & secundum) separates right and left atria.

b: Close to bronchial tree – important for congenital airway anomalies
sections.p: Anteriorly the heart contacts the sternum; posteriorly the esophagus and thoracic aorta. The pericardial cavity contains a small amount of fluid that lubricates movement.

b: Right coronary artery supplies right ventricle and SA node
Left coronary artery supplies left ventricle and AV node
sections.p: Coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses after septation. Early embryonic heart relies on diffusion from the yolk sac before coronary vessels develop.

b: Vagal tone dominates in fetal life, protecting against tachyarrhythmia
sections.p: Autonomic innervation reaches the heart via the cardiac plexus; sympathetic fibers increase rate and contractility, parasympathetic (vagus) slows the heart.
The mature heart provides a continuous, coordinated pump delivering oxygenated blood systemically and deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

b: Ventricular septal defect – loud holosystolic murmur, left‑to‑right shunt
Atrial septal defect – fixed split S2, risk of paradoxical emboli
Tetralogy of Fallot – cyanosis, boot‑shaped heart on X‑ray
sections.p: Errors in looping or septation produce common congenital lesions seen in low‑resource settings, often presenting with cyanosis, heart failure, or murmurs.

t.b: Confirms anatomy of septal defects; if unavailable, rely on clinical murmur, chest X‑ray, and oxygen saturation trends
Detects cyanosis; a reading <90 % suggests right‑to‑left shunt
Shows cardiomegaly or characteristic silhouettes (e.g., boot‑shaped heart in TOF)

b: Assess peripheral pulses – weak or delayed in severe outflow obstruction
Look for clubbing – chronic hypoxia from uncorrected shunts
Measure blood pressure in both arms – difference suggests coarctation
sections.p: When examining a newborn or child with suspected cardiac malformation, focus on cyanosis, feeding difficulty, growth failure, and auscultation of murmurs.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe cyanosis or oxygen saturation <85 % in a newborn
Rapidly worsening heart failure signs (pulmonary edema, hepatomegaly)
Sudden collapse after a murmur is heard – possible ductus arteriosus closure
